props.title: Wait Until Dark
props.initialSlug: Blind woman outwits criminals in deadly home game

sections.content: Wait Until Dark (1967) revolutionized the home invasion thriller by masterfully playing with darkness and vulnerability. Audrey Hepburn delivers a career-defining performance as Susy Hendrix, a blind woman terrorized by criminals searching for a heroin-filled doll. The film's genius lies in how director Terence Young gradually builds tension through Susy's spatial awareness of her apartment, culminating in that legendary sequence where she breaks all the lights to level the playing field against Alan Arkin's ruthless Harry Roat. This influenced later confined-space thrillers like Panic Room (2002) and Don't Breathe (2016). Dial M for Murder|1954|Hitchcock's claustrophobic thriller about a husband plotting his wife's murder in their apartment, featuring Grace Kelly|Prime Rear Window|1954|James Stewart plays a wheelchair-bound photographer who suspects his neighbor of murder|Prime The Silence of the Lambs|1991|FBI trainee Clarice Starling hunts a killer in darkness using night vision, creating similar tension|Netflix

The confined setting thriller reached new heights in the 1960s with films like Wait Until Dark and Repulsion (1965). These movies transformed ordinary apartments into psychological battlegrounds, where familiar spaces become threatening mazes. The genre continued evolving through Rosemary's Baby (1968), which similarly trapped its protagonist in an apartment with sinister neighbors, and later Pacific Heights (1990), where homeowners face a manipulative tenant. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Disability in Thrillers

Wait Until Dark stands out for its groundbreaking portrayal of a disabled protagonist who turns her perceived weakness into strength. This paved the way for more nuanced portrayals in films like See No Evil (1971) and Julia's Eyes (2010). Rather than treating blindness as merely a plot device, these films explore how their protagonists' other senses become heightened in life-threatening situations. The influence extends to modern thrillers like Hush (2016), featuring a deaf protagonist, and A Quiet Place (2018), where silence becomes both vulnerability and weapon.
